summary.value: Symptoms begin as small whitish or yellowish flecks or blotches on the upper leaf surface that enlarge with black specks inside; these specks merge into irregular black stomata 0.5 to 3.0 mm in diameter surrounded by a yellow-white band of dead tissue.

diagnostic_features.value: Raised black fungal fruiting bodies (stromata) form within the leaf spots, giving the leaf a bumpy texture as if dotted with tar; black specks merge into single irregular stomata 0.5 to 3.0 mm in diameter surrounded by a yellow-white band of dead tissue, and successive seasons of twig blighting can cause witches' broom.
diagnostic_features.quote: These fungal structures are raised and will give the leaf a bumpy texture. As more spots develop and coalesce, they will create white areas of dead tissue that can eventually turn brown.

value: Remove infected leaf debris and dead shoots; rake up leaf litter and prune out infected stems to remove inoculum for the following season.

treatments.quote: Management of this disease includes removing infected leaf debris and dead shoots. Avoid overhead irrigation and close spacing of cuttings and young trees. pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Dutch elm disease is caused by two closely related fungi, Ophiostoma ulmi and Ophiostoma novo-ulmi.

type_of_disease.quote: An invasive fungal pathogen causes the disease and occurs throughout Minnesota.

value: Foliar
Stem
Vascular
Root
Whole plant
affected_parts.quote: Leaves on one or more branches in the outer crown of the tree turn yellow, wilt and then turn brown. ... Once in the tree's vascular system, the fungal spores are carried up the tree with the flow of water. ... the fungus can reach the root system in the first season of infection. ... Dutch elm disease (DED) causes wilt and death in all elm species native to Minnesota.

summary.value: Yellow foliage appears on one or more branches in the outer crown from late spring to midsummer, soon becoming wilted and brown ("flagging"), with yellowing and wilting progressing down the infected branch toward the trunk; fallen leaves may be strewn over the lawn in spring or summer.
summary.quote: The first symptom observed in American elm is yellow foliage on one or more branches, from late spring to midsummer. The affected foliage soon becomes wilted and brown; this symptom is called "flagging."

diagnostic_features.value: Wilted and brown foliage on individual branches called "flagging," with brown discoloration/streaking of the sapwood visible when the bark is removed on recently wilted branches.
diagnostic_features.quote: If the bark is removed, brown streaking can be seen along the sapwood of wilted branches.

value: Manage by eliminating bark beetle breeding sites: promptly remove dead or dying elm wood with intact bark.
Remove DED-infected branches the same year infection starts, before the disease moves into the main stem, cutting at least 5 feet (preferably 10 feet) below the last sign of streaking in the sapwood.
Properly dispose of elm wood by burying, debarking, burning, or chipping.
Sever root grafts between infected and adjacent elms (e.g., with a vibratory plow or trenching to 3-4 feet deep) before removing the infected tree.
Take down trees with many infected branches.
Choose Dutch elm disease-resistant cultivars for new or replacement plantings.
Preventative fungicide injection treatments (e.g., thiabendazole, propiconazole) can protect highly valuable trees, but are expensive and regarded as a temporary measure.
Without community-wide sanitation, Dutch elm disease is almost impossible to control.
treatments.quote: Reduce the number of breeding sites available to the beetles by promptly removing dead or dying elm wood with intact bark. ... Fungicides with the active ingredients thiabendazole and propiconazole are effective against DED.

web_support.quote: Dutch elm disease is a vascular wilt of elms; a diagnostic feature is the formation of brown streaks in infected sapwood revealed when bark is removed, rather than external cankers or fruiting structures.
When the bark is peeled or cut on infected branches, longitudinal, brown-colored bands or streaks in the outer rings of the sapwood are almost always visible.

web_support.quote: The diagnostic feature is brown streaking in infected sapwood seen when bark is removed; the microscopic fruiting bodies of the fungus are not visible in the field.
Dutch elm disease is a vascular wilt; symptoms are foliar wilt/flagging and internal sapwood discoloration rather than external cankers or conspicuous fruiting bodies on the bark.

web_support.quote: As the pathogen spreads out of the infected branch, larger areas of the crown begin to rapidly wilt resulting in crown dieback, with complete wilting sometimes within a few months.
For many American elms, once a branch becomes symptomatic, adjacent branches also quickly show symptoms, followed by major canopy dieback (Sinclair and Lyon 2005).
